paras: The Putnam County church burnings were the burning of five Black churches, two schools and a lodge hall near Dennis Station, outside Eatonton in Putnam County, Georgia, in the spring of 1919, attributed to a party of white men said to have revived the Ku Klux Klan. No one was reported killed in the fires, and no report of an arrest appears in the coverage. Black weeklies across the country carried the story under headlines naming the Klan, and Black editorials cited it among the year's outrages against Black Americans.

According to the Associated Negro Press (ANP), the outbreak was said to have begun with a clash at Dennis Station, near Eatonton, between an unknown Black man and a white merchant. The man asked for a bottle of soda as the merchant was closing his store and was refused; he was "alleged to have made some remarks" about courtesy on a hot night, which the merchant resented. Companions of the Black man then took up the quarrel, pistols appeared and many shots were exchanged, with no fatalities.

Afterward, five churches, two schools and a lodge hall in Putnam County were set on fire at almost the same hour, which the ANP said pointed to concerted action by a party of white men. Among the buildings destroyed was Ward Chapel, described as more than a hundred years old and situated in a community where William H. Seward had once taught school. The exact date of the fires does not appear in the coverage, but the Boston Transcript had already commented on them in its issue of June 2, as quoted by the Cleveland Advocate.

A mass meeting of white residents raised $1,000 as a reward for running down those who set the fires, and a similar amount was asked of Governor Hugh Dorsey. White residents also raised money to rebuild; the ANP put the sum at "several thousand dollars," while an Atlanta item in the Cleveland Advocate reported $3,000 raised toward a goal of $5,000. The destruction was condemned in mass meetings of both races. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial was found.

Most Black papers received the story through an ANP dispatch from Macon, dated June 10 in the Phoenix Tribune and June 12 elsewhere, which ran in the St. Louis Argus, the Black Dispatch, the Dallas Express, the Phoenix Tribune and, as late as July 5, the National Advocate. Headlines put the Klan forward: "Kuklux Klan Rages in Dear Old Georgia" in the Black Dispatch, "Ku Klux on Rampage in Georgia" in the Dallas Express and "Ku Klux Klan at Work in Georgia" in the National Advocate, while the Argus headline stressed that white citizens were raising money to rebuild. The National Advocate appended its own comment: "Another case of locking the stable after the horse is gone. This is what we receive by making the world safe for democracy."

A separate dispatch from Eatonton, printed by the Chicago Defender on June 21 and the Colorado Statesman on June 28, described "the terror of the Ku Klux Klan" at Dennis Station and blamed "a band of outlaws" calling themselves the Klan. The Cleveland Advocate reprinted a Boston Transcript editorial that called the burnings a "stroke of pure race resentment against the upward climb of another race" and set them beside recent mob violence in New Haven. The Omaha Monitor cited the fires as proof that "the enemies of true democracy are organized and at work," and the Colorado Statesman listed the burning of "homes and churches" by "a present-day Ku Klux Klan" at "Eaton, Ga." among recent outrages.

On the investigation, the ANP reported that officers claimed to have made a thorough search and found no clues, while the Eatonton dispatch said the perpetrators were "said to be known" but that local authorities were afraid to arrest them for fear of defeat in the next election. The Atlanta item in the Cleveland Advocate counted six churches rather than five and put the reward at $1,100 rather than $1,000. The Omaha Monitor's June 19 reference to the fires as happening "last week" does not fit the Transcript editorial of June 2.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press (Macon)
accounts.gist: Five churches, two schools and a lodge hall fired at almost the same hour by a party of white men who had revived the Klan, after a soda-store quarrel and shooting at Dennis Station; officers found no clues; whites raised a reward and rebuilding money.

accounts.label: Eatonton correspondent
accounts.gist: Klan terror at Dennis Station burned the buildings; perpetrators are said to be known but local authorities fear to arrest them lest they lose the next election.

accounts.label: Atlanta item
accounts.gist: Six churches burned by a white mob; white citizens subscribed $1,100 reward and $3,000 of $5,000 for rebuilding.

accounts.label: Boston Transcript editorial (quoted)
accounts.gist: The burning of five churches and two schoolhouses was pure race resentment that no region could approve; Georgia was expected to punish the perpetrators.

framing.detail: ANP headlines in Black weeklies named the Klan ('Kuklux Klan Rages in Dear Old Georgia', 'Ku Klux on Rampage in Georgia', 'Ku Klux Klan at Work in Georgia'), and the National Advocate added that it was 'what we receive by making the world safe for democracy.'
The Eatonton dispatch charged that known perpetrators went unarrested because local officials feared the voters.
Omaha Monitor and Colorado Statesman editorials cited the Klan burnings as signs of organized reaction against Black Americans after the war.
The Boston Transcript, as quoted by the Cleveland Advocate, called the burnings 'pure race resentment against the upward climb of another race.'
